jokotoba.text: 八重むぐら しげれる宿の さびしきに
jokotoba.function: Describes the overgrown, weed-choked dwelling and its desolation in exhaustive physical/sensory detail, building the atmosphere of abandonment that the shimo-no-ku's emotional revelation (the arrival of autumn, confirmed by absence of visitors) depends upon. Though it functions much like a scene-setting description rather than a purely sound-driven jokotoba, it occupies the full kami-no-ku and pivots into the shimo via the desolation established.

honkadori.source_poem: Traditionally associated with the Kokinshū-era topos of the overgrown dwelling (yaemugura shigereru yado) as used by Ariwara no Yukihira and echoed later by Ryōkan/other poets; most directly this poem itself is often cited as source material for later verses, but no single confirmed Man'yōshū/Kokinshū source poem can be identified with full confidence.
honkadori.echoed_phrase: 八重むぐらしげれる宿
honkadori.function: Evokes the conventional image of a hermit's or recluse's overgrown, weed-choked residence as a marker of solitude and withdrawal from society, a well-established topos in Heian poetry of reclusion.

kigo.note: 秋 (autumn) is the explicit seasonal marker and the poem's emotional and structural climax: its arrival is perceived not through any visible seasonal sign but through the negative proof of nobody visiting the overgrown dwelling. This inverts the conventional kigo function — autumn is normally announced by wind, dew, or changing leaves, but here it is confirmed purely inferentially through human absence, giving the season itself a melancholic, almost personified weight tied to the yamazato (mountain hermitage) topos of solitude.

bipartite.kami_theme: A physical description of a dwelling overrun with the weed yaemugura (eightfold creeper), so thickly overgrown that it has become desolate and lonely — a scene of physical neglect and abandonment.
bipartite.shimo_theme: Though no human visitor ever appears, the speaker perceives that autumn has arrived — the season itself becomes the poem's true 'visitor,' discovered through solitude rather than through any visible sign of foliage or wind.
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku's description of overgrown desolation does not directly depict autumn at all; instead the shimo-no-ku pivots on the discovery that, amid total human absence, the only presence detectable is the season itself. The poem's meaning depends on holding these together: the absence of people (kami's desolation intensified) becomes proof, by contrast, of the presence of autumn — an inference from isolation to seasonal awareness, rather than any direct causal or visual link.

source_jp:
八重むぐら
しげれる宿の
さびしきに
人こそ見えね
秋は来にけり
